To advance the technology readiness level, the project team has identified the following next steps:  Extended-duration testing to evaluate material wear, electrode erosion, and carbon- deposition behavior over continuous operation exceeding 1,000 hours.  Control-system integration to enable automatic plasma modulation based on real-time engine load, fuel flow, and exhaust feedback.  System optimization through refinement of electrode geometry, flow-field distribution, and Southwest Research Institute® U.S. DOE Award Number DE-FE0032301 Public Version - 21 - DE-FE0032301 Final Report power-delivery algorithms to maximize conversion efficiency at higher flow rates.  Field demonstration on a commercial midstream compressor engine to confirm methane leak reductions under real-world duty cycles and environmental conditions.  Technology-transfer and commercialization partnerships with industry collaborators are being pursued to support advancement from TRL 5 toward TRL 7. In parallel, SwRI will continue to explore applications of the core pulsed-power technology for hydrogen-enriched combustion, exhaust aftertreatments, and non-thermal plasma chemical processing, leveraging the platform’s scalability and a low-cost modular design. 5.5 Public Executive Summary Southwest Research Institute (SwRI) designed and demonstrated a compact, plasma-based fuel reformer designed to reduce methane leaks from natural-gas engines used in pipeline compression and industrial power applications. The system uses pulsed electrical discharges to convert a small portion of methane (CH ) into hydrogen (H ) and light hydrocarbons, promoting 4 2 more complete combustion and reducing unburned methane in the exhaust. The reformer was evaluated through bench-scale testing, high-flow facility testing, and engine-integration testing on representative low-speed and high-speed natural-gas engines. Measured methane-leak reductions ranged from 1 to 27 percent, depending on engine type and operating condition, while reformer energy consumption remained below one percent of total engine output. Design refinements addressed thermal and electrical challenges, resulting in reliable operation with minimal impact on engine control systems. The project achieved all performance objectives within budget and schedule, produced a patentable pulsed-power system design, and established a scalable, energy-efficient pathway for mitigating methane leaks from existing natural-gas engine infrastructure.
